query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that integrates actively‐learned machine‐learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with a configurational averaging method (such as CPA) and explicit inclusion of defect chemistry (in particular, ~1 wt.% oxygen impurities) will yield more accurate electrical conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr, in both the cryogenic (0–200 K) and high temperature (300–1200 K) regimes, compared to conventional analytical models that assume perfect, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a single-phase BCC structure produced by conventional methods, but realistically containing extended defects and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
generation.intervention: Use an integrated simulation framework that employs actively learned MLIPs to capture local relaxations (including defect-induced lattice distortions) combined with CPA to account for compositional disorder and finite-temperature vibrational effects.
generation.conditions: Simulations and subsequent predictions performed over two temperature ranges: near cryogenic temperatures (0–200 K) where defect dynamics are essentially frozen and minimal phonon excitations occur, and elevated temperatures (300–1200 K) where thermal excitations and defect mobility can influence electronic scattering.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic relaxations around oxygen impurities and other defect sites, as well as the inhomogeneous microstructures (e.g., reported one‐dimensional Ta-rich features) that alter the electronic band structure and scattering mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly incorporating defect-induced local lattice distortions and temperature-dependent relaxation effects via MLIP and CPA methods, the approach can modulate the predicted electronic density of states and transport scattering rates. This better captures the impact of nonideal microstructures and oxygen incorporation on conduction pathways relative to the ‘ideal’ crystal assumption.
generation.predicted_outcome: The conductivity predictions will show improved agreement with experimental measurements (i.e. lower prediction errors) in both temperature regimes. For instance, in the 0–200 K regime, the model is expected to capture conductivity plateaus or subtle changes due to defect freeze-out effects; whereas in the 300–1200 K regime, it will reflect the gradual softening and increased phonon-electron scattering effects. Overall, the predictive error is expected to be reduced by roughly 30–50% compared to conventional analytical predictions.
generation.baseline: Analytical predictions based on ideal, defect-free BCC HfNbTaTiZr that presently overestimate conductivity accuracy by neglecting impurity effects and local relaxations.
generation.boundary: The improved predictive accuracy is anticipated to hold for single-phase, BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloys with oxygen impurity concentrations near 1 wt.%; predictions may deviate if oxygen levels or phase inhomogeneities exceed this range or if additional phases (e.g., HCP precipitates) emerge under extreme processing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement factors and precise conductivity values remain uncertain due to the complexity of defect-defect interactions and potential microstructural evolution during thermal exposure. The effectiveness of the MLIP-CPA integrated method in fully capturing these phenomena across the full temperature range needs experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr specimens via a method that yields a controlled oxygen level (~1 wt.%) and measure their low-frequency electrical conductivity over the two specified temperature regimes (0–200 K and 300–1200 K). Simultaneously, perform conductivity predictions using both the proposed MLIP-CPA integrated approach and conventional analytical models. The experiment should include detailed microstructural and defect characterization (via TEM, XRD, and oxygen quantification) to confirm the sample state.
measurements: Electrical conductivity as a function of temperature (spectroscopy or four-point probe measurements) in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges
Defect density and oxygen content analysis
Comparison of predicted conductivity values with measured data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated predictive approach does not reduce the prediction error by at least ~30% relative to conventional analytical models across both temperature regimes, or if the predicted conductivity temperature dependence fails to reflect the experimentally observed behavior (e.g., misrepresenting defect freeze-out or thermal scattering effects), the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In conclusion, we have demonstrated how a combination of CPA and actively-learned MTPs can solve the problem of predicting the CRSS and intrinsic ductility of refractory MPEAs over the whole composition space with ab initio accuracy, a problem that is currently not tractable with conventional ab initio-based methods. In particular, by integrating our ab initio automated workflow into a robust Bayesian multi-objective optimization framework we have applied the developed approach to identifying high-performance Pareto-optimal compositions. Furthermore, our supercell size convergence tests enabled by MTP-powered molecular statics have revealed that sizes of typical supercell sizes used in conventional SQS calculations are often insufficient for accurate calculations of certain important materials properties, such as the surface energy, of multi-component alloys. Specifically, the surface energy of MoNbTi has been shown to exhibit a rather slow convergence with the supercell size, which leads to errors of 10–20% for SQS supercells of about 100 atoms.

HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy was produced by various methods of powder metallurgy including mechanical alloying, sintering, hot isostatic pressing, spark plasma sintering, and high pressure torsion. The microstructure and mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr prepared by various methods were examined. It was found that the main problem in fabrication of HfNbTaTiZr alloy by powder metallurgy is oxygen contamination. Samples prepared by cold isostatic pressing followed by sintering and/or hot isostatic pressing contained oxygen in the concentration range of 0.55 wt %–0.85 wt %. Oxygen contamination of samples prepared by mechanical alloying was even higher, and the oxygen concentration in these samples exceeded 1 wt %. Oxygen incorporated into the HfNbTaTiZr samples caused deterioration of mechanical properties (embrittlement) and prevented formation of a single phase random solid solution. Investigations performed in the present work showed that the most promising powder metallurgy method of production of HfNbTaTiZr alloy was spark plasma sintering of gas atomized powder. cited_evidence.text: Ab-initio MC simulation was performed to evaluate the microstructure stability of investigated alloys. Simulation was performed for the 5 element HfNbTaTiZr alloy, because it contains all elements considered in investigated alloys. Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, Zr ions were distributed randomly in equimolar concentration into a 250 atom BCC supercell. This initial state was relaxed with respect to ion positions until minimum of the total free energy was reached. The equilibrium configuration corresponding to minimum free energy was obtained using a Metropolis MC algorithm at 300 K (room temperature). The details of the simulation and more complete results will be published elsewhere. Figure 7 shows the equilibrium atomic configuration corresponding to the minimum of total energy. The most apparent effect is a rather one-dimensional Ta object (‘wire’) along the <100> direction. The Ta wire is surrounded predominantly by Nb ions. The rest of the simulation box is filled up by the mixture of Ti, Zr and Hf. The latter two elements appear to be well separated from the Ta and Nb region.
